To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the ACT College Outcome Study (ACT COS) data failed to provide empirical support for the claims that US undergraduate education has failed to generate high levels of student intellectualism or career preparation, or that such education has failed to produce such growth for first generation and minority students.

(a) there was no significant difference in the levels of intellectual growth and career preparation between our two samples of graduates; (b) there was a significant difference in the level of intellectual growth between our two samples, such that our sample of minority and/or first generation students had a significantly higher level of intellectual growth than our sample of white and/or first generation free students; and (c) there was no difference in the level career preparation between our samples of minority and/or non first generation students, and

(1) the average college graduate has experienced more intellectual growth in college than he or she has career development, (2) the average first generation and minority graduate has experienced less intellectual growth in college that the average non first generation and non minority graduate, and (3) the average first and minority graduate has not experienced significantly more career development than the average non first and non minority graduate.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the extent to which US colleges have failed (1) to generate substantial levels intellectualism among their students, (2) to generate a substantial level of intellectualism among first generation and minority students, and (3) to generate a high level of career preparation among their students.
a question of considerable interest: Do US colleges generate high levels of intellectual growth and career preparation?
the extent to which colleges have been successful in enhancing student career preparation and intellectualism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ACT College Outcome Study is a very useful instrument for the measurement of college outcome variables, but it is not without its limitations.
the results of this study do not provide support for the claims of critics who assert that US colleges have largely failed to foster substantial levels of intellectual growth and career preparation.

the ACT data do not provide any empirical support for the assertion that the US college system has generated a relatively low degree of intellectualism or career preparation among its first generation and minority students.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that colleges do not fail their first-generation and minority students in terms of intellectual growth.
the ACT data does not support the claim that colleges have failed to develop intellectualism among their students, and have failed to provide their students with career preparation.
we have found no evidence that colleges have failed to provide a significant level of intellectualism and/or career development among their graduates.
